articles.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation for the treatment of recurrent Clostridioides difficile (Clostridium difficile).
articles.snippet: Minkoff NZ, Aslam S, Medina M, Tanner-Smith EE, Zackular JP, Acra S et al. | The Cochrane database of systematic reviews | 2023-Apr-25 | Systematic Review; Journal Article; Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural
articles.full_summary: FMT likely increases resolution of recurrent C. difficile infection in immunocompetent patients and may slightly reduce serious adverse events.
articles.key_finding: Pooled results from six studies showed that the use of FMT in immunocompetent participants with rCDI likely leads to a large increase in resolution of rCDI in the FMT group compared to control.
articles.population: immunocompetent adults with recurrent C. difficile infection

articles.title: Faecal microbiota transplantation for first or second Clostridioides difficile infection (EarlyFMT): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.

articles.full_summary: First-line FMT is highly effective and superior to vancomycin alone for sustained resolution of first or second C. difficile infection.
articles.key_finding: 19 (90%; 95% CI 70-99) of 21 patients in the faecal microbiota transplantation group and seven (33%, 95% CI 15-57) of 21 patients in the placebo group had resolution of CDAD at week 8 (p=0·0003).
articles.population: patients with first or second C. difficile infection

articles.title: Faecal microbiota transplantation for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis.

articles.full_summary: FMT is effective for recurrent C. difficile infection, with repeat FMT and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy delivery showing superior results.
articles.key_finding: The overall clinical effect week 8 following repeat FMT (24 studies, 1855 patients) was 91% (95% CI: 89-94%, I 2=53%) and 84% (80-88%, I 2=86%) following single FMT (43 studies, 2937 patients).
articles.population: patients with recurrent C. difficile infection

articles.title: Reset of a critically disturbed microbial ecosystem: faecal transplant in recurrent Clostridium difficile infection.
articles.snippet: Fuentes S, van Nood E, Tims S, Heikamp-de Jong I, ter Braak CJ, Keller JJ et al. | The ISME journal | 2014-Aug | Journal Article; Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.full_summary: This randomized controlled trial investigates the mechanism of action of FMT in recurrent CDI by analyzing changes in faecal microbiota composition and diversity.
articles.key_finding: All patients successfully recovered. Their intestinal microbiota changed from a low-diversity diseased state, dominated by Proteobacteria and Bacilli, to a more diverse ecosystem resembling that of healthy donors, dominated by Bacteroidetes and Clostridium groups, including butyrate-producing bacteria.

response.global_summary:
Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is an effective treatment for recurrent *Clostridioides difficile* infection (rCDI), with high cure rates reported across various study designs and patient populations [0][1][2][3][5][6][7][9]. Current guidelines recommend FMT for preventing multiply recurrent CDI after two recurrences, with cure rates approaching **90%** [6].

Several studies demonstrate the efficacy of FMT. A 2022 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (the *EarlyFMT* trial) involving patients with first or second *C. difficile* infection found that **90%** (19 of 21 patients) in the FMT group achieved resolution of *C. difficile*-associated diarrhoea at week 8, compared to **33%** (7 of 21 patients) in the placebo group (*p*=0.0003) [1]. A 2023 systematic review of six studies in immunocompetent adults with rCDI concluded that FMT likely leads to a large increase in resolution of rCDI compared to control groups [0]. Similarly, a 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis reported an overall clinical effect at week 8 of **91%** following repeat FMT (across 24 studies, 1855 patients) and **84%** following single FMT (across 43 studies, 2937 patients) [2].

Real-world data and cohort studies further support these findings. A 4-year retrospective cohort study in Switzerland found that among 88 patients receiving 100 FMTs, clinical cure was achieved in **93%** after a single treatment, **98%** after two, and **100%** after three treatments [5]. Another cohort study in a Dutch population reported an FMT cure rate for rCDI of **92.8%** (77 of 83 patients), with six early recurrences within two months post-FMT [7]. A case report on the use of lyophilized oral capsules for FMT in patients with recurrent CDI showed a primary cure rate of **81.3%** and an overall cure rate of **87.5%** [9].

FMT appears to restore a healthy gut microbiota. A 2014 randomized controlled trial observed that patients successfully recovered and their intestinal microbiota shifted from a low-diversity diseased state, dominated by Proteobacteria and Bacilli, to a more diverse ecosystem resembling that of healthy donors, dominated by Bacteroidetes and *Clostridium* groups, including butyrate-producing bacteria [3]. Despite variations in methodological approaches for providing FMT, clinical outcomes in terms of cure rates appear to be remarkably similar [8].

key_findings.text: Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is highly effective in treating recurrent *Clostridioides difficile* infection (rCDI), with cure rates often exceeding 80% and approaching 90% or more across various studies and patient populations.
FMT can lead to a significant increase in the resolution of rCDI compared to placebo or standard antibiotic therapy.
The efficacy of FMT has been observed in immunocompetent adults with rCDI, as well as in patients with first or second *C. difficile* infection.
FMT helps restore the diversity of the intestinal microbiota, shifting it from a diseased state to one resembling that of healthy donors, with an increase in beneficial bacteria.
Repeat FMT may achieve higher cure rates than single FMT, with one systematic review reporting 91% for repeat FMT versus 84% for single FMT.
Clinical cure rates for FMT can reach 93% after a single treatment, and even higher (98-100%) after multiple treatments.
Current guidelines recommend FMT for the prevention of multiply recurrent *Clostridioides difficile* infection after two recurrences.

evidence_gaps: These sources do not provide detailed information on the long-term safety profile of FMT beyond the reported cure rates and early recurrences.
The specific optimal number of FMT treatments for all patients is not definitively established, although some sources suggest higher cure rates with repeat treatments.

The sources do not extensively compare the efficacy of different administration routes for FMT (e.g., colonoscopy, oral capsules, enema) in a head-to-head manner, beyond noting similar outcomes despite methodological variations.
The sources do not provide specific data on the efficacy and safety of FMT in immunocompromised patients, as one systematic review focused on immunocompetent participants.
